lessons.title: How Indians Access Commodity Markets: MCX, ETFs, and Related Equities

children.text: Three Routes Into a Commodity Cycle

Understanding a cycle is only half the job. The other half is knowing which instrument actually gets you exposure to it, from India, without taking on risk you did not intend to take. Broadly, there are three routes: direct futures contracts on the Multi Commodity Exchange, listed ETFs and bonds for gold and silver, and equity proxies for oil and industrial metals, where India does not offer a retail commodity ETF at all. Which route makes sense depends entirely on which commodity you are dealing with, and this lesson maps that out before Chapters 2 to 4 get specific.
Route 1: MCX Futures, the Direct Route

The Multi Commodity Exchange, MCX, is India's main commodity derivatives exchange, regulated by SEBI since the erstwhile Forward Markets Commission was merged into it in 2015. On MCX, you can trade futures contracts on crude oil, natural gas, gold, silver, copper, zinc, aluminium, nickel and lead, among others, through a commodity trading account with a broker such as Zerodha, exactly the way you would trade equity futures on the NSE.

A futures contract is a leveraged instrument. You post a margin, a fraction of the contract's full value, and your position is marked to market daily, meaning gains and losses are settled into or out of your account every single day the position is open. Most MCX contracts you will trade as a retail investor settle in cash against a benchmark price on expiry, rather than requiring you to take physical delivery of barrels of crude or bars of copper, though a few contracts do offer physical delivery for participants who want it.

body.text: Leverage cuts both ways. A contract that requires, say, five to ten percent margin gives you roughly ten to twenty times exposure relative to your capital. A price move that would be a rounding error for someone holding the physical commodity can wipe out a large share of your margin in a single session. Exact margin requirements are set and revised by the exchange and your broker, so always check the current specification before placing a trade rather than relying on a number from a course or an old screenshot.

body.caption: Broad MCX Contract Categories (Check MCX's Current Circulars for Exact Lot Sizes and Margins)

cells: Full-size and smaller Mini/Guinea-type contracts for different capital sizes
Cash-settled against an international benchmark price
Traders taking a view on the oil cycle without importing or refining anything themselves
Cash-settled, tracking London Metal Exchange-linked pricing
Traders and some industrial hedgers with metal input costs

children.text: Route 2: Gold and Silver Have a Ready-Made ETF and Bond Route

Gold is the one commodity in this course with a genuinely simple access route for a long-term investor. Gold ETFs, run by asset managers such as HDFC, SBI, Nippon India and ICICI Prudential, hold physical gold in a vault and issue units that trade on the NSE and BSE like a stock. Buy a unit through your regular demat account, and you own a claim on physical gold with none of the storage or purity worries of buying jewellery or coins. Silver ETFs work the same way and have been available in India since regulatory approval in 2021 to 2022.

Sovereign Gold Bonds, SGBs, are a different structure entirely: a government bond, issued by the RBI on behalf of the Government of India, denominated in grams of gold. Holders earn a fixed cash interest on top of whatever the gold price does, and if held to maturity, capital gains for an individual investor are exempt from tax, a feature no other gold instrument in India offers. Outstanding SGBs continue to trade on the exchange even in periods when the government pauses fresh issuance, so check the RBI's current issuance calendar before assuming a new tranche is open, but existing bonds remain a live way to gain gold exposure.

body.label: SGB Capital Gains at Maturity
body.context: This applies only if the bond is held to its full maturity, typically eight years from issue. Selling on the exchange before maturity attracts capital gains tax like any other listed security.

children.text: Route 3: Oil and Industrial Metals Run Through Equity Proxies

There is no spot ETF for crude oil or industrial metals listed in India, the way there is for gold. Beyond MCX futures, which are a trading instrument rather than a buy-and-hold one, most investors get exposure to the oil and metals cycles indirectly, through listed companies whose earnings move with the commodity. This is a real trade-off: you gain the convenience of a normal equity investment, but you also inherit company-specific risk, debt, management quality, that has nothing to do with the commodity cycle itself.

body.caption: Equity Proxies for Oil and Metals on the NSE and BSE

cells: Oil marketing companies: IOC, BPCL, HPCL, whose marketing margins and inventory can get squeezed
Producers: Tata Steel, JSW Steel, Hindalco, Vedanta, NALCO, Hindustan Zinc
Metal-consuming manufacturers: autos, capital goods and consumer durables makers who buy steel or aluminium as raw material

children.text: This table is a starting map, not a complete one, and it is worth re-checking on screener.in before you act on it: a company's actual sensitivity to a commodity price depends on its specific business mix, hedging policy and balance sheet at that point in time, all of which change.

body.title: Before You Trade a Commodity Future on MCX
steps: Confirm the current lot size and margin requirement for that specific contract with your broker or on the MCX website
Check the contract's expiry date and whether it is cash-settled or allows physical delivery
Work out your maximum acceptable loss in rupees before entering, given the leverage involved, not just the price level you expect
Understand that your position is marked to market daily, so a losing trade can trigger a margin call before the underlying story even plays out
Decide in advance whether you will roll the position to the next contract month or let it expire

cards.definition: Multi Commodity Exchange, India's main exchange for commodity futures, regulated by SEBI.
Sovereign Gold Bond, a government bond denominated in grams of gold, issued by the RBI, paying fixed interest plus gold price appreciation.
The daily process of settling a futures position's gains or losses into or out of your account, based on that day's closing price.
The gap between an ETF's return and the return of the physical asset it is meant to track, arising from fund expenses and cash drag.
A listed company used to gain indirect exposure to a commodity price, because a direct instrument in that commodity is unavailable or impractical.

points: MCX futures give direct, leveraged exposure to nearly every commodity in this course, but they are a trading instrument, not a buy-and-hold one, and leverage magnifies losses as fast as gains.
Gold, and now silver, have a genuinely simple buy-and-hold route through ETFs, with Sovereign Gold Bonds adding a tax-exempt-at-maturity option on top.

Oil and industrial metals have no retail spot ETF in India. Exposure runs through equity proxies, upstream producers and OMCs for oil, metal producers for industrial metals, which adds company-specific risk on top of the commodity cycle.
Whichever route you use, verify current contract specifications, margin rules and a company's actual commodity exposure before acting, since all three change over time.
